title: Days of the week — and respect that comes in the plural
title_target: आपका हफ़्ता कैसा होता है? — aapkaa haftaa kaisaa hotaa hai?
goal: Talk about your week and ask about other people's — while learning why Indians refer to one person as "they", and discovering that Hindi day names, like English ones, are named after the planets.
bekal: name the seven days and twelve months
use the respectful plural for older people
use से … तक for time spans
ask about other people's jobs and schedules

dialogs.title: संवाद — How's your week?
dialogs.intro: Ani asks what Priya's family keeps busy with. In line five she catches something that may have been nagging you since unit 5: why Priya refers to her own mother with a word that means "they".

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.literal: your — father — ji — what — doing — are?

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: He works at a bank. He leaves at nine every day.
lines.literal: they — bank — in — work — doing — are. daily — nine — o'clock — going — are.

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: She's at home. She gets up very early.
lines.literal: they — home — at — staying(fem.) — are. morning — early — getting-up(fem.) — are.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: A question — why do you say "ve"? She's only one person.
lines.literal: one — question — you — "they" — why — saying(fem.) — are? they — (stress) — one — only — are.

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: For older people we always use the plural. Out of respect.
lines.literal: elders(obl.) — of — for — we — always — plural — speaking — are. respect — of — for.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Got it. And what's your week usually like?
lines.literal: understand — went(fem.). and — your — week — how — being — is?

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: Monday to Friday, college. Saturday off.
lines.literal: Monday — from — Friday — until — college. Saturday — on — holiday.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: What do you do on Sunday?

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.literal: something — not! afternoon — until — sleeping(fem.) — am.

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: Yes, one day a week. The other days there's lots of work.

notes: **Respect in Hindi is plural, and that goes for the third person too.** You already know आप takes हैं. The same rule applies when you **talk about** someone you respect: *वे मेरे पिता जी **हैं***, *माँ जी घर पर **हैं***, *डॉक्टर साहब **आते हैं***. ⚠️ Using the singular for your own parents — *मेरे पिता जी है* — sounds both wrong and slightly rude.

**Who gets this respect?** Parents and in-laws, teachers, bosses, people much older than you, guests, and anyone you're not close to yet. For friends your age, younger siblings, and children, the singular is what's natural — using the respectful form with a close friend sounds cold, as if you were keeping your distance.

**इज़्ज़त — honor, dignity, good name.** It's related to Arabic *izzah*, and in Hindi-Urdu it's a heavy word: *इज़्ज़त की बात है* ("it's a matter of honor") is said in earnest. Compare **सम्मान**, its more formal and cooler Sanskrit equivalent.

**Every day name ends in -वार, and the origin will feel familiar.** वार means "day". In front of it is a Sanskrit planet name: **रवि** (Sun), **सोम** (Moon), **मंगल** (Mars), **बुध** (Mercury), **गुरु** (Jupiter), **शुक्र** (Venus), **शनि** (Saturn). ⚠️ If that system sounds familiar, it is: English *Sunday*, *Monday*, *Saturday* and French *mardi* (Mars), *mercredi* (Mercury), *vendredi* (Venus) follow **exactly the same planetary week**. The seven-planet week traveled both east and west, and the day names are its most durable trace.

**Sunday has two names: रविवार and इतवार.** The first is Sanskrit, the second comes from Persian. Both are everyday words, इतवार a bit more casual. It's a perfect example of the two vocabulary layers described at the front of the book — and the same pattern shows up in **हफ़्ता** (Persian) vs. **सप्ताह** (Sanskrit) for "week", **ज़बान** vs. **भाषा** for "language", **शुक्रिया** vs. **धन्यवाद**.

**से … तक covers every span, of time or place.** *सोमवार **से** शुक्रवार **तक*** (Monday to Friday), *सुबह **से** शाम **तक*** (morning to evening), *दिल्ली **से** आगरा **तक*** (Delhi to Agra). ⚠️ Note that both are postpositions, so the noun goes oblique: *कमरे से छत तक*.

**छुट्टी is one of the most useful words in India.** It means holiday, day off, and leave all at once. *आज छुट्टी है* (today's a holiday), *मुझे छुट्टी चाहिए* (I need time off), *छुट्टी पर हूँ* (I'm on leave). And because India celebrates festivals of several religions, ⚠️ **the Indian calendar has far more holidays than you'd expect** — check it before making important plans.

grammars.title: Days, months, and time spans
after: ⚠️ Day names always take **को** when you say something happens on that day: *शनिवार **को** छुट्टी है*. Month names don't: *मैं जनवरी में आऊँगी*.

grammars.title: The respectful form: one person, plural verb
after: ⚠️ Note that **gender still shows**: वे आ**ते** हैं for a man, वे आ**ती** हैं for a woman. Only the number changes, not the gender. So you still need the rule from unit 4.

sections.title: Describing your day and your week

blocks.text: Build your routine story from the pieces below. Swap the verbs from the unit 4 list, swap the times from unit 9, and you can talk about your whole week without a single new word.

head: Time
Example sentence
Meaning
rows: आठ बजे मैं काम पर जाती हूँ।
At eight I leave for work.
एक बजे मैं खाना खाती हूँ।
पाँच बजे मैं घर आती हूँ।
शाम को मैं हिंदी पढ़ती हूँ।
In the evening I study Hindi.
रात को मैं परिवार से बात करती हूँ।
At night I call my family.
At eleven I go to bed.

blocks.title: Linking words that turn it into a story
items: **फिर** (*phir*) — then, next. The most common one.
**आख़िर में** (*aa-khir meⁿ*) — finally, in the end.
**आम तौर पर** (*aam taur par*) — usually. Handy for opening a routine story.
⚠️ Linking words go **at the start** of the sentence, not at the end like the verb: *फिर मैं नाश्ता करती हूँ*, not *मैं नाश्ता करती हूँ फिर*.

blocks.text: One exercise that really works and takes just five minutes: before bed, tell yourself about your day in Hindi — slowly, aloud, in simple sentences. It doesn't have to be perfect. What works isn't accuracy but **repeating the sentence pattern**: subject first, verb last, time words in between. In two weeks that pattern will come out without thinking, and that's the whole point of the exercise.

exercises.prompt: Write the day names in Hindi.
Choose the respectful or the ordinary form.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

My father works in an office.
I get up at six, then I have breakfast.

answers: आपका हफ़्ता कैसा होता है? — शनिवार को छुट्टी है। — वे बैंक में काम करते हैं। — मैं दोपहर तक सोती हूँ। — मैं आठ बजे काम पर जाती हूँ।

मेरे पिता जी दफ़्तर में काम करते हैं। — मेरी माँ सुबह जल्दी उठती हैं। — सोमवार से शुक्रवार तक मैं काम करती हूँ। — रविवार को छुट्टी है। — मैं छह बजे उठती हूँ, फिर नाश्ता करती हूँ। — आपका हफ़्ता कैसा होता है?
